analysis.one_liner: Lets workers and consumers take race discrimination claims to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after being referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2023, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Many employers and companies require workers and customers to sign agreements saying that any discrimination dispute goes to a private arbitrator chosen under company-friendly rules, rather than a public court, and bans joining class actions. This bill would let a person alleging race discrimination — including harassment or retaliation based on race, color, or national origin — choose to go to court instead, and to join class actions. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and consumers who face race, color, or national origin discrimination, harassment, or retaliation and want their day in a public court. Because arbitration is hidden and often cheaper for companies to win, people alleging race discrimination frequently get small private settlements with no public record; a court case, or a class action, creates accountability that arbitration does not. The bill does not ban arbitration outright — it lets the person alleging discrimination choose court instead, at the election of the worker or consumer, not the company.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and customers alleging race discrimination

how_it_helps.text: It voids predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for race discrimination disputes, when the person alleging discrimination chooses court.
It gives workers the option of joining class or collective actions, where one lawyer can represent many workers at once — often the only realistic way to challenge a widespread practice.
It requires a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether the law applies, and applies to any claim arising after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and businesses that use arbitration agreements would lose a key legal shield for race discrimination claims: cases could become public court trials, and class actions would be harder to block. Companies would likely face higher litigation costs and more public scrutiny of discriminatory practices. The general public bears none of the cost; there is no spending or tax provision in the bill.

drawbacks.text: Employers and businesses argue that arbitration resolves disputes faster and more cheaply than court litigation, and that removing it for race claims will increase litigation costs.

The bill is narrow: it covers only race, color, and national origin discrimination claims, leaving forced arbitration in place for many other types of disputes — including sex, disability, and age discrimination claims by consumers and some workers — so many people remain bound by arbitration agreements.
The bill only voids predispute agreements; a company and a worker could still agree to arbitrate after a dispute arises, which could invite settlement pressure on workers already in a weak position.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is meaningful: it would restore access to public courts for the workers and consumers least able to enforce their rights, closing a loophole left by a 2022 law that covered sex discrimination but not race. The main costs are efficiency ones — some cases that could be resolved quickly and cheaply in arbitration will take longer in court, and employers and consumers may respond with more paperwork and tighter contracts. No serious objection in the record addresses the core unfairness the bill targets, but the narrow scope (race only, not other discrimination) means many similarly situated workers remain excluded.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in May 2023 and never advanced — no hearing, no vote — until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on May 2, 2023, with Senators Gillibrand and Durbin.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that require workers and customers to sign arbitration agreements keep the ability to force race discrimination claims into private arbitration and block class actions. Arbitration providers keep their case volume.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void forced arbitration for race discrimination claims.

for.name: Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand and Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

for.name: 12 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate majority never brought it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill died in a Democratic-held Senate without a vote.

industries.industry: Employers and companies that require arbitration agreements
industries.note: Employers could no longer force race discrimination claims into private arbitration or block class actions, exposing them to public court cases and collective suits. The bill was referred to committee and died, so their current protections remain intact.
Arbitration firms earn fees on employment and consumer disputes; exempting race discrimination cases removes a stream of cases, though only if the bill passes. It did not.

industries.industry: Defense law firms built on arbitration and class-waiver enforcement
industries.note: Corporate defense practices that enforce arbitration agreements and defeat class certification would see fewer such tools in race discrimination cases. The bill's death preserves the status quo.
